title: How Ranked Choice Voting Works
summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about a recent trip to Australia and New Zealand, then turn to ranked choice voting (also called instant runoff voting). They explain how ballots are ranked and tallied in rounds, contrast it with plurality winner-take-all voting, and cover the 2000 Florida recount and Ralph Nader spoiler debate, Maine's 2018 adoption and governor's veto, the history of ranked choice voting in New York City in the 1930s and Burlington, Vermont, Oakland's 2010 mayoral race, ballot exhaustion, and criticisms about cost and complexity. The episode closes with a listener email from a retired NYPD detective about double-blind lineups and witness testimony.
topics: New York City 1937 city council election

segments.title: Opening banter and Australia trip
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about movies, sports, and their recent ten-flight trip to Australia and New Zealand, including Melbourne, Sydney, and the Mornington Peninsula.

segments.title: Australia as a ranked choice voting user
segments.summary: Josh notes Australia, Malta, and Ireland use ranked choice voting, and says the system has roots tied to Robert's Rules of Order. He transitions into the US context.

segments.title: 2000 election and the spoiler problem
segments.summary: Josh recounts the 2000 presidential election, the Florida margin between Bush and Gore, and the popular vote versus electoral college split. The hosts discuss Ralph Nader being blamed as a spoiler, and how plurality voting can hand an election to a least-favored candidate.

segments.title: How ranked choice voting works
segments.summary: The hosts explain ranking candidates on a ballot, and that if no candidate has a majority, the last-place candidate is eliminated and their votes redistributed to next choices in successive rounds, also called instant runoff voting.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A short break for sponsor messages before the show continues.

segments.title: Polarization, centrism, and incentives
segments.summary: The hosts argue that winner-take-all elections encourage polarizing campaigns, while ranked choice voting rewards candidates for appealing to a broad base. They note a Kansas primary decided by under 200 votes and discuss whether centrist politicians would be favored and the ideological split of voters.

segments.title: Maine's adoption and governor's veto
segments.summary: Maine's record of governors elected with under 50 percent is discussed, along with Governor Paul LePage's veto of a ranked choice voting bill, his stated cost and process objections, and the earlier voter referendum that approved keeping the system. The hosts also mention higher turnout and a University of Missouri study.

segments.title: Ranked choice voting history: New York and Burlington
segments.summary: The hosts describe earlier American use of ranked choice voting in New York, where a 1937 city council election elected a Communist, followed by repeal. They also cover Burlington, Vermont, where the system was repealed after a mayoral scandal.

segments.title: Oakland 2010, ballot exhaustion, and criticisms
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Oakland's 2010 mayoral race, where Jane Kim won after rounds of redistribution despite trailing in first-choice votes, and San Francisco's top-three ranking. They cover ballot exhaustion rates from a 2015 study and the debate over whether ranking every candidate is better.

segments.title: Trump, primaries, and wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts speculate how a ranked choice primary in 2016 might have changed the Republican field, referencing a Bloomberg View column, and conclude that the system is worth trying while urging listeners to learn more.

segments.title: Listener mail: retired NYPD detective on lineups
segments.summary: A retired NYPD detective writes about double-blind lineups, photo arrays being inadmissible as trial evidence in New York, defense lawyers' role at lineups, and the limited value of witness testimony compared to other evidence.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank listeners, invite contact through social media and email, and sign off.
